title: Diffusion arrival
response: Choose one route. Point, say, sign, draw, type or write. You may pass or say not sure. Use the screen or paper; you do not need to do both.
access: Nothing here assumes you have met diffusion before. The questions use everyday ideas about smells, drinks and breathing; an adult can read them to you or write your words.
staff: Allow four minutes within the arrival stage. Read or scribe as needed. Start from what pupils show; a pass or a not-sure is information about the starting point, not a label. Accept spoken, signed, drawn, pointed, chosen or scribed answers as equal.

supported.label: Supported
questions: Someone opens a bottle of perfume at the front. Can people at the back smell it after a while? Yes / No.
Two glasses of squash: one strong, one weak. Which one has more squash particles in the same amount of water? Strong / Weak.
In a gas, are the particles close together or far apart? Close / Far apart.
When you breathe in, where does oxygen get into your blood? Lungs / Stomach.
answers: Yes. Accept pointing or nodding. The smell spreads through the air on its own.
Strong. More particles in the same volume means a higher concentration.
Far apart, and moving. Accept a gesture that shows spread-out particles.
Lungs. The air sacs in the lungs are where oxygen enters the blood.

standard.label: Standard
questions: A smell spreads across a still room. What is actually moving from the bottle to your nose?
What does the word concentration mean when we talk about a solution or a gas?
Particles move in solids, liquids and gases. In which state do they move most freely?
Name the gas that our blood collects in the lungs and the gas it gives up there.
answers: Particles of the perfume, mixed into the air. Accept molecules.
How many particles of a substance there are in a given volume. Accept how much is dissolved in a certain amount.
Gases; the particles are far apart and move freely in all directions.
Oxygen is collected; carbon dioxide is given up.

stretch.label: Stretch
questions: A smell reaches the back of a still room. Explain what makes the particles spread when nothing is pushing them.
Two areas have different concentrations of the same substance. What name do we give to that difference?
Why do particles in a warm gas spread out faster than particles in a cold gas?
Oxygen passes from the air sacs of the lungs into the blood. Suggest why it goes that way and not the other.
answers: Particles move randomly all the time. Over time random motion carries more of them from where they are crowded to where they are few, so the smell spreads. Accept a first idea to refine later.
A concentration gradient. Accept the difference in concentration between two places.
Warm particles have more energy and move faster, so they spread out more quickly.
There is more oxygen in the air sac than in the blood arriving there, so the net movement is into the blood. Accept from high to low concentration.
